newsitem.title: USA: BP aims to boost presence in U.S. market.
newsitem.headline: BP aims to boost presence in U.S. market.

text.p: British Petroleum Plc is looking to boost its profile in the U.S. market, BP group chief executive John Browne said Wednesday.
"We're very keen to expand our presence here," he told a group of reporters after he spoke at a British-American Business Association lunch.
BP America, with 35 percent of BP Plc's assets, accounted for almost one-third of the corporation's 1996 operating profits.
Focusing on oil and natural gas production, the company was looking to increase output in Alaska, where it is the biggest producer, and in deep waters in the Gulf of Mexico.

Browne said the Gulf division, starting from a small base, was one of the fastest growing parts of the company, with production expected to rise to 75,000 barrels per day this year from 60,000 bpd, and reach 200,000 bpd around the turn of the century.
Although production from Alaska's biggest field, Prudhoe Bay, was falling, Browne said production from new fields would halt the decline within a year or two.
"The overall net production to BP will be considerably enhanced (in Alaska)," he said. "As a result it will stop declining in the next year or so."

Browne said although the company was not necessarily able to garner good prices for its Alaska North Slope crude in the Far East, the U.S. move to lift a 23-year-old ban on Alaskan oil exports last year was good for the company.
"It's very important that we have more than one market to sell any product," he said.
"While you can say that sometimes the prices aren't that good, you have to say that's not the point. It is the longer run market," he said.
BP was satisfied for the moment with its strong regional presence in refining and marketing. "At the moment we like that position very much," Browne said.
Because of BP's interests in the United States, Browne said the company was very wary of U.S. foreign sanctions policy.
He told the British-American Business Association that U.S. sanctions had worked to limit industry investment in Iran.
But BP had "no burning passion" to do business in Iran and had seen no worthwhile opportunities there ever since it had been expelled from Iran.
